title: A first-principles theory of turbulent transport

concept.text: The proposed innovation is a theory that derives the statistical behavior of turbulent incompressible fluids from their governing equations and specified physical inputs. Instead of resolving every fluctuation, it would predict quantities such as drag, momentum transport and the distribution of kinetic energy across scales, together with informative error bounds. Initial conditions, forcing and boundary conditions would remain necessary inputs; the ambition is to eliminate empirically adjustable closure constants, not the information that defines the physical problem.

A closure supplies relationships needed when equations for averaged fluid motion contain unknown effects of turbulent fluctuations. The target could take the form of a derived closure or an equivalent statistical solution theory. Its defining advance would be reliable prediction in high-Reynolds-number flows and unfamiliar geometries without fitting the closure to those validation experiments. Reynolds number characterizes the relative importance of inertia and viscosity; extending the theory toward arbitrarily large Reynolds number is an ambition whose validity would require mathematical justification beyond finite tests.

significance.text: If computationally usable, such a theory would make turbulent transport a substantially more predictive part of engineering. Within its demonstrated domain, designers could calculate drag and fluctuation statistics for previously untuned flows with defensible uncertainty estimates. Spalart’s 2023 discussion establishes both the engineering usefulness of existing turbulence models and their difficulties with generality. Existing models can retain fixed core constants across applications, so the advance should not be described as eliminating a new fitted constant that every present model requires for every geometry. The stronger goal is reliable prediction despite changes in flow conditions and geometry.

Conditional implications: successful pipe-flow, isotropic-turbulence and additional-geometry demonstrations would support practical uses within the physical and numerical domain they establish. Broader applications to wings, turbines, scalar mixing and geophysical transport would also require tractable computation and suitable treatment of boundaries, compressibility, rotation, stratification or coupled scalar transport. Weather and climate prediction would additionally depend on moisture, radiation, boundary and initial data, and other coupled processes. These applications are possible extensions of the proposed capability, not automatic consequences of passing the initial benchmarks.

The distinction from the Navier–Stokes existence-and-smoothness problem is fundamental. Establishing that solutions remain smooth, or that a permitted forcing can cause a breakdown of the specified solution properties, does not by itself calculate drag, mixing or fluctuation statistics. Such mathematical results could have indirect consequences for turbulence theory, but neither alone supplies the proposed transport law or guarantees long-term weather prediction. This distinction follows from the different mathematical objectives of the official problem and statistical transport prediction.

missing_breakthrough.text: The central target is a controlled derivation connecting the incompressible equations to useful statistical predictions at high Reynolds number. The theory must determine the effects of unresolved fluctuations without inserting empirical relationships whose reliability is unknown in the new flow. It must also state which initial, forcing and boundary data its predictions depend on, what assumptions it makes, and where its error estimates apply. Spalart’s paper documents the empirical modeling and generalization problems motivating this target; that historical evidence does not establish that every equivalent capability remained unavailable on 1 November 2026.

Concrete barriers include controlling closure approximations, obtaining informative errors in the high-Reynolds-number regime, transferring predictions between geometries, and keeping the resulting calculation affordable. A formally derived expression would have limited engineering value if its errors were too loose to distinguish designs or if evaluating it required impractical computation. The theory must therefore connect mathematical validity, statistical averaging and usable numerical prediction rather than succeed on only one of these fronts.

Machine learning can assist model construction, but fitting a learned closure does not alone establish a first-principles statistical theory. Spalart describes model choices, overfitting risks and unpredictable extrapolation outside a studied training interval. These are specific reasons to demand prospective validation and clear validity conditions, not evidence that every possible learning-based method must fail. A future learned component would need an independently justified role and errors consistent with the proposed theory’s claims.

current_state.text: Spalart’s paper, posted on 1 August 2023, documents useful engineering turbulence models alongside empirical choices, computational constraints and weaknesses in prediction outside familiar conditions. It also discusses generality and well-understood limiting behavior at very high Reynolds number as modeling goals. This provides substantive evidence for the problem motivating MAT-03, but does not establish the state of every competing approach at the record’s 1 November 2026 assessment cutoff. The supplied research contains no populated search record resolving that freshness question.

The earlier research invokes Kolmogorov’s 1941 scaling and high-but-finite Reynolds numbers in direct numerical simulation as background. The supplied evidence review did not have adequate inspected support to substantiate those descriptions, distinguish the scaling argument from a derivation of anomalous exponents in detail, or report a numerical simulation frontier. Those points therefore remain background claims requiring suitable sources; their evidentiary limits do not demonstrate that the claims are false.

Fefferman’s official Navier–Stokes formulation offers four alternative existence-and-smoothness or breakdown statements. Statements (A) and (B) set the external force to zero. Statements (C) and (D) permit smooth forcing subject to the formulation’s specified decay or periodicity conditions and seek failure of the required global solution properties. This is a question about the mathematical behavior of solutions, distinct from deriving their turbulent transport statistics.

The retained Clay Mathematics Institute announcement dated 11 September 2026 describes an apparent settlement of the Navier–Stokes problem and a deliberately unhurried evaluation process. That dated announcement does not independently establish proof correctness, identify the proof’s author in the supplied review, or resolve its exact coverage. The earlier research also attributes a claimed proof of statements (C) and (D) to an OpenAI posting dated 8 September 2026, but that page was not captured for the review. Its date, authorship attribution and claimed theorem scope remain unverified in this record. The supplied material also does not establish whether a prize had been awarded by 1 November 2026.

In a March 2025 arXiv preprint, Yu Deng, Zaher Hani and Xiao Ma present derivations of compressible Euler and incompressible Navier–Stokes–Fourier limits from dilute hard-sphere dynamics through Boltzmann’s equation under specified assumptions, including periodic-domain settings. The Navier–Stokes–Fourier result fixes a smooth fluid solution on the interval considered. This is a substantial connection between particle dynamics and continuum equations, but it does not supply a high-Reynolds-number statistical turbulence closure. The review could examine the relevant introductory theorem statements; the retained PDF ends during page 34, so it did not provide a complete extracted paper. Publication or subsequent validation beyond the supplied preprint is not established here.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration: derive predictions from the governing equations and specified physical inputs for both the friction coefficient of smooth-pipe flow and the kinetic-energy spectrum of homogeneous isotropic turbulence. Test each across at least three decades of a clearly defined Reynolds number, with informative error bounds and no closure constant fitted to those validation experiments. Define the Reynolds-number conventions for each flow explicitly. The three-decade range is a proposed benchmark for this record, not an established scientific standard.
completion_criteria.label: Predict pipe friction and isotropic spectra across three Reynolds-number decades

completion_criteria.text: Proposed prospective validation: predict a preregistered flow of different geometry, such as flow over a periodic hill, before inspecting its validation data. Specify forcing, geometry, boundary conditions, statistical averaging, numerical convergence requirements and acceptance tolerances in advance. Error bounds should be sufficiently narrow to test useful predictions, rather than accommodate nearly any outcome. This proposal addresses the generalization problem discussed by Spalart, but its exact protocol is not prescribed by that source.
completion_criteria.label: Predict preregistered flow in different geometry before inspecting validation data

completion_criteria.text: Proposed reproducibility and practical boundaries: make the derivation, assumptions, numerical implementation and validation procedure available for independent replication. Separate errors from the theory, numerical approximation and validation measurements. Report computational cost and identify the supported range of Reynolds numbers, geometries and physical effects. Passing these finite tests would demonstrate substantial breadth, not literal universality or validity at arbitrarily large Reynolds number; stronger claims would need additional mathematical results or validation. A single scaling exponent, an empirical learned fit, or a singularity proof alone would not meet this proposed demonstration.
completion_criteria.label: Enable independent replication with separated errors and reported practical limits

related_concepts.text: Roster comparison—MAT-04, Proved polynomial-cost solution of high-dimensional nonlinear PDEs: this has the closest computational overlap because turbulent-flow predictions must ultimately be calculated from equations or their statistical consequences. A proved efficient PDE solver could aid MAT-03, but efficiency alone does not establish a general transport closure, informative statistical errors or transfer between geometries. Conversely, a successful statistical transport theory need not solve the broad class of high-dimensional nonlinear PDEs envisaged by MAT-04.

Roster comparison—MAT-07, A prescriptive mathematical theory of deep learning: the overlap concerns principled model construction, generalization and uncertainty when learning is used for turbulence closures. MAT-07 would address learning systems more broadly; MAT-03 requires predictions grounded in fluid equations and specified physical data. A theory of learning could strengthen a closure’s justification without itself deriving turbulent transport.

Roster comparison—MAT-05, Research-scale machine-checked mathematical discovery: automated discovery and verification could assist derivations and check claims in turbulence theory. They concern the process and reliability of mathematical research, while MAT-03 concerns a particular physical predictive capability. Machine-checking an existence or breakdown proof would not, by itself, produce transport statistics.

Roster comparison—MAT-08, Polynomial-time chemical accuracy for molecular electronic structure: both seek controlled, practically useful predictions from governing physical laws. Their physical objects and bottlenecks differ: molecular electronic structure concerns electronic calculations, whereas MAT-03 concerns turbulent statistics in incompressible fluids. The hard-sphere derivation discussed here is a particle-to-continuum result and does not merge either target with the other.

Roster comparison—MAT-01, Practical polynomial-time algorithms for NP-complete problems; MAT-06, Classical polynomial-time integer factorization and discrete logarithms; and MAT-09, Classical polynomial-time algorithms for cryptographic lattice problems: these are distinct algorithmic targets. Their shared relevance is the aspiration to make difficult calculations tractable, but the supplied material establishes no reduction or implication connecting any of them to turbulent transport. MAT-02, An effective global Langlands correspondence over number fields, is also a separate mathematical program; no direct technical connection is supplied. All remain independent roster entries.

brief.title: Reliable predictions of turbulent fluid motion
possible: Engineers could predict how much a turbulent flow resists motion and how its energy spreads across different sizes of swirl, even in unfamiliar shapes. The predictions would follow from fluid equations and specified physical conditions, with useful error bounds and without tuning constants to match the test results.
why: Designers could compare designs with a clearer account of how much to trust their calculations. Reliable predictions across changing shapes and flow conditions would make turbulence a more predictable part of engineering.

sources.showed: Spalart describes how useful engineering models still depend on empirical choices. He identifies overfitting and poor prediction outside familiar conditions as obstacles for models built with machine learning.
sources.quote: Very few of the ML papers produced models which could be coded  by others, or which had clear hopes of being general.
sources.cited_for: Existing models motivate the need for predictions that remain reliable across different flows.
sources.not_established: This assessment does not derive turbulent statistics from fluid equations.

sources.showed: Fefferman defines the mathematical question of whether fluid equations always retain smooth solutions or can break down. He also reviews partial results.
sources.quote:
In three dimensions, it is known that (A)
and (B) hold provided the initial velocity u◦ satisﬁes a smallness condition.
sources.cited_for: Proving that fluid equations remain smooth or break down addresses a different question from predicting turbulent transport.
sources.not_established: These mathematical results do not calculate drag or the statistics of turbulent fluctuations.

sources.showed: OpenAI reports a proof that a smooth external force can drive initially resting fluid toward unbounded speed in finite time. It also reports a formal proof written for computer checking.
sources.quote: Our system produced an analytical proof and a Lean formalization that an initially smooth fluid at rest can develop a singularity in a finite time.
sources.cited_for: A claimed breakdown of smooth fluid motion is distinct from a theory that predicts turbulent statistics.
sources.not_established: The claimed proof remains subject to mathematical evaluation and does not supply a turbulent transport law.

sources.showed: The institute announces an apparent settlement of the fluid-equation smoothness problem and says mathematical evaluation will proceed deliberately.
sources.cited_for: The announced mathematical solution was still undergoing evaluation.
sources.not_established: The announcement does not establish proof correctness or a method for predicting turbulent transport.

sources.who: Yu Deng, Zaher Hani and Xiao Ma
sources.showed: In a preprint, the authors derive fluid equations from idealized colliding particles under specified assumptions. Their result for fluids that do not compress assumes a smooth fluid solution over the period considered.
sources.quote:
In this paper, we rigorously derive the fundamental PDEs of fluid mechanics, such as the com-
pressible Euler and incompressible Navier-Stokes-Fourier equations, starting from the hard sphere particle
systems undergoing elastic collisions.
sources.cited_for: Fluid equations can be connected mathematically to underlying particle motion.
sources.not_established: Deriving fluid equations from particles does not derive useful statistics for strongly turbulent flows.

shown: Engineering turbulence models already provide useful calculations. Spalart describes their successes alongside empirical choices and difficulties predicting unfamiliar flows.

Deng, Hani and Ma connect particle motion to fluid equations in a preprint. OpenAI reports a proof of mathematical breakdown under smooth forcing. Neither result supplies the statistical predictions sought here.
missing: The target is a derivation of turbulent statistics for fluids that do not compress, using specified starting conditions, forces and boundaries.
Useful error bounds must hold at high Reynolds number, where inertia—the tendency of motion to continue—outweighs internal friction.
Predictions must transfer to unfamiliar shapes without tuning constants to the validation results.
The calculations must be affordable enough to compare engineering designs.

milestones.label: Pipe friction and energy across swirl sizes
milestones.explanation: Theory would have to predict smooth-pipe friction and energy across swirl sizes in uniform turbulence with no preferred direction over a thousandfold Reynolds-number range, without tuning. Useful error bounds would make this a meaningful test.

milestones.label: An advance prediction in a different shape
milestones.explanation: A test registered in advance would have to predict flow in a different shape before its comparison data are examined, with conditions and acceptance limits fixed. This would test whether the theory works beyond familiar flows.

milestones.label: Independent reproduction with costs and limits
milestones.explanation: Independent teams would have to reproduce the results, separating theory, calculation and measurement errors while reporting costs and supported conditions. This would establish reproducibility and practical reach.

uncertain: The proposed flow range is a benchmark choice; precise definitions, averaging rules and acceptance tolerances remain to be settled.
Success in finite tests would not establish validity at arbitrarily large Reynolds number.
Extensions to wings, turbines or geophysical flows would require suitable treatment of additional physical effects.

page.title: First-principles theory of turbulent transport
page.definition: A statistical theory derives drag, momentum transfer and velocity fluctuations of incompressible turbulent fluids from their governing equations at high Reynolds number, where inertia dominates viscosity. It supplies derived closure relations—the extra relationships needed after averaging—with bounded prediction errors.

goal.need: Skin friction accounts for about 50% of civil-aircraft drag in cruise. For NASA’s hump benchmark at chord Reynolds number 936,000, typical Reynolds-averaged models overpredict separation-bubble length by about 35% and underpredict peak turbulent shear-stress magnitude by about 45%. These quantities connect turbulent momentum transport to design calculations.

figures.caption: NASA hump benchmark: documented errors in typical Reynolds-averaged predictions
figures.note: Baseline flow without control; Mach number 0.1 and chord Reynolds number 936,000. These are benchmark-specific errors.

statements.quote: physics-based, accurate predictions of complex turbulent flows, including flow separation
statements.context: The study identifies this capability as an objective for computational analysis and design; it does not require an empirically unfitted statistical theory.

statements.quote: scientists still cannot reliably predict how complex turbulent systems behave across vastly different scales.
statements.context: The announcement of 26 August 2026 establishes TEMPEST to develop physics-grounded turbulence models, covering fluids and plasmas.

completion.title: Independent experiments validate a derived turbulent-transport theory in an unfamiliar geometry.
completion.criterion: An independent group tests a peer-reviewed derivation from incompressible Navier–Stokes equations by predicting drag and velocity-fluctuation statistics in a geometry outside its initial validation flows. No empirical closure parameter is fitted to that experiment. Measurements agree within combined theoretical, numerical and experimental uncertainty specified before comparison. The derivation bounds statistical prediction errors for the tested Reynolds numbers, forcing, boundaries and averaging; uncertainty intervals are narrower than measured variation across conditions. Achievement covers this stated domain.
completion.set_by: Atlas fallback; no outside completion criterion was found for this combination of derivation, error control and transfer between geometries.
completion.basis: Searched NASA’s CFD roadmap and prediction-error challenge, NSF’s TEMPEST objectives, AIAA-linked benchmark materials, Spalart’s modeling requirements and Sreenivasan–Schumacher’s solution criteria. None defines this completion test. The latter states: “There is no single problem that can be regarded universally as constituting the turbulence problem.” The test combines statistical derivation with independent transport prediction within a finite domain.

milestones.title: A turbulence theory recovers the four-fifths law under its stated assumptions.
milestones.criterion: For three-dimensional homogeneous, isotropic turbulence in the inertial range, recover ⟨(δu_L)³⟩ = −(4/5)εr, where δu_L is the longitudinal velocity difference across separation r and ε is mean energy dissipation per unit mass. State the stationarity and inviscid-limit assumptions, including the dissipation assumption. This conditional result dates to 1941. Moisy and colleagues reported on 17 May 1999 that the forced Kolmogorov equation agreed with helium-gas measurements within ±3% over microscale Reynolds numbers 120–1,200; that finite-Reynolds-number test does not prove the limiting assumptions.
milestones.set_by: Community convention: Kolmogorov’s four-fifths law; its use as an acceptance condition is documented by Cerbus and Chakraborty, quoting Frisch.
milestones.threshold_quote: must either satisfy the four-fifths law, or explicitly violate the assumptions made in deriving it.

milestones.title: A Reynolds-averaged model reduces NASA hump prediction error by 40%.
milestones.criterion: Apply NASA’s 40% prediction-error reduction target to its published hump separation-bubble metric at Mach 0.1 and chord Reynolds number 936,000. The metric is the relative error in bubble length, whose experimental value is 0.435 times hump chord; the documented typical error is about 35%. A 40% reduction corresponds to about 21% error. NASA permits judgment in metric selection; this is one benchmark target. Its 2016 report also shows wall-modeled large-eddy simulation matching experimental reattachment at x/c = 1.1, without establishing a first-principles closure.
milestones.set_by: NASA Revolutionary Computational Aerosciences and Transformational Tools and Technologies programmes; 40% Challenge and Standard Test Cases, applied here to the published hump bubble-length metric.
milestones.threshold_quote: 40% reduction in predictive error against standard test cases for turbulent separated flows

milestones.title: A derived closure predicts laboratory transport with error bounds that resolve measured changes.
milestones.criterion: Derive a closure or equivalent statistical solution from incompressible Navier–Stokes dynamics with specified physical inputs. In its initial laboratory validation flows, predict drag and velocity-fluctuation statistics without empirical closure fitting; bound prediction errors over the stated Reynolds-number and averaging ranges, with intervals narrower than measured variation across conditions. Independent transfer remains the completion test. Warnecke’s preprint of 12 March 2026 reports a three-point statistical interpolation compared with preliminary simulations; it does not report this transport-error demonstration.
milestones.set_by: Atlas fallback: the reviewed statistical-theory literature, NASA roadmap and Spalart requirements contain no acceptance threshold for this controlled-error derivation and laboratory demonstration.

results.detail: The supplied text says the viscous term may be neglected at large separation, but does not state the stationarity or inviscid-limit dissipation assumptions. Its transcription also obscures the coefficient in equation (7).

results.finding: For stationary 3D Navier–Stokes solutions (sample size not applicable), the paper derives a 4/5-law limit under weak anomalous dissipation.
results.detail: The result assumes homogeneity, approximate inertial-range isotropy and weak anomalous dissipation as viscosity tends to zero. Its ε is mean energy input; the paper assumes only an energy inequality, so it does not establish that ε equals mean energy dissipation. Existence of solutions satisfying its weak dissipation assumption remains open.
results.quote:
If the force is statistically homogeneous, then any homogeneous martingale solution satisfies the spherically averaged 4/5 law pointwise in space.
An additional hypothesis of approximate isotropy in the inertial range gives the traditional version of the Kolmogorov law.

results.detail: The error is below the approximately 21% target, and the report states Mach 0.1. However, the supplied text does not state the chord Reynolds number, so the specified condition cannot be verified. The model was calibrated using this hump case.
